newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels in talks, govt concession reported.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels in talks, govt concession reported.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages were due to start a fourth round of talks later on Monday to try and end the 69-day-old crisis peacefully, as a Japanese newspaper reported a major official concession.
Mainichi Shimbun said President Alberto Fujimori had agreed to include the rebels' main demand -- the release of jailed comrades -- on the agenda in the negotiations.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa also discussed improving jail conditions for 400 MRTA prisoners at a meeting on Thursday, according to Mainichi Shimbun, quoting a source close to the talks.
One possible government concession discussed was allowing the prisoners more family visits, the source said.
A government spokesman told Reuters he could not comment on the newspaper report.
The rebel demand for the release of prisoners has been the main stumbling block in talks with the government, although congressmen hinted last week that a deal might be in sight.

Those imprisoned include 27-year-old American woman Lori Berenson, who is serving a life sentence in a grim jail 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) up in the Andes after being convicted by a "faceless" military court of plotting an assault on Congress.
Hopes of progress were raised on Thursday when Cerpa left the the Japanese ambassador's Lima residence to meet Palermo face-to-face.

It was the first time Cerpa had left his stronghold since he led his well-armed guerrillas to seize hundreds of hostages in a spectacular assault on a cocktail party to celebrate the Japanese emperor's birthday on Dec. 17.
In the initial three meetings, Cerpa was represented by his deputy, Rolly "The Arab" Rojas, who conferred with his chief via a specially installed telephone hotline.

Fujimori told reporters that Cerpa's presence had helped Thursday's talks make "a small advance" towards a peaceful solution to the siege. But he added the guerrilla leader spent part of his hour-long address to Palermo slamming the government.
Guarantors of the negotiations from the Roman Catholic Church and the Canadian embassy said Thursday's session had broached "important issues", but gave no more details.
There was no guarantee that Cerpa would attend the fourth round of talks in a nearby safehouse behind police roadblocks.

On Sunday, heavily-armed police continued their psychological war against the guerrillas, blaring an incongruous mix of songs and tunes through powerful speakers aimed at the residence. The day's musical lineup veered from Beethoven and opera sung by Placido Domingo to the theme from "Love Story" and "Take My Breath Away" from Hollywood movie "Top Gun".

Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani entered the residence to say a mass, and Red Cross medical staff gave the hostages -- many of whom are suffering from treatable maladies typical of middle-aged men -- a check-up.
The rebels, who freed most of their haul of captives in the early days of the crisis, have now beaten the previous record for Latin America's longest-ever hostage siege by a week.

The guerrillas have boobytrapped the building with bombs, and their hostages include the president's younger brother Pedro, as well two government ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
